subsection: 6. The suffrage movement and educational reforms

notes.b: Irish women campaigned for the vote from the 1870s, first through local societies and later through local government reform.
points: Isabella Tod founded a women’s suffrage society in Belfast in 1872, the first of its kind in Ireland (about the first in Ireland, verify).
Anna Haslam and her husband Thomas Haslam founded the Dublin Women’s Suffrage Association in 1876, later renamed the Irish Women’s Suffrage and Local Government Association.
The Haslams and Tod campaigned for women’s property rights, girls’ education and the vote for women ratepayers in local elections.
The Local Government (Ireland) Act of 1898 allowed women to stand for and sit on poor law boards and rural district councils, giving women a public local role.

notes.b: Tod was a Belfast suffragist and unionist who linked women’s rights with social reform and with the Union.
points: Isabella Tod (1836–1896) was a Belfast campaigner who worked for women’s suffrage, married women’s property rights and girls’ education.
As a participant she organised suffrage meetings and petitions in Belfast, and she founded the Belfast suffrage society in 1872.
Contemporaries in Belfast saw her as a respected philanthropist whose campaigning was accepted within the Protestant middle class.
Tod’s unionism shaped her suffrage work: she believed women’s rights should be secured within the Union, and she opposed Home Rule.
Historians now see Tod as a pioneer of organised Irish feminism, and her work in Belfast is often compared with the Dublin campaign of the Haslams.

notes.h: The Irish Women’s Franchise League and militancy (1908–1912)
notes.b: The Irish suffrage movement grew more militant after 1908, and in 1912 Dublin women used window-breaking and hunger strikes in the suffragette style.
points: The Irish Women’s Franchise League was founded in 1908 by Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington and Margaret Cousins, with a platform of votes for women on the same terms as men.
The League was separate from the Irish Party, which opposed women’s suffrage, and its members argued that the Home Rule Bill should include votes for women.
The term suffragette was used by the British press for militant campaigners, and the Irish League adopted similar tactics after 1912.
In 1912 Irish suffragettes broke windows in Dublin during the visit of Prime Minister Asquith, who had been expected to speak in favour of women’s suffrage.
Suffragettes imprisoned in Dublin in 1912 went on hunger strike and were force-fed, which provoked public debate over the treatment of women in custody.
Suffragists were divided over nationalism and unionism, and the movement had little support from the Irish Party, whose leaders Redmond and Dillon opposed women’s suffrage.

notes.b: Sheehy-Skeffington was a leading Irish feminist and pacifist, who combined suffrage campaigning with a commitment to nationalist and socialist causes.
points: Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington (1877–1946) was a founder of the Irish Women’s Franchise League and a leading suffrage campaigner in Dublin.
As a participant, she led the militant Dublin campaign in 1912 and was jailed for the protests, which contributed to the militancy of the period.
Contemporary suffragists and nationalists were divided over her: some admired her commitment to women’s rights, while others saw her as a threat to the unity of the movement.
She married Francis Sheehy-Skeffington in 1903, and she and her husband promoted feminism alongside a nationalist and pacifist position.
Francis Sheehy-Skeffington was killed by a British army officer, Captain J.C. Bowen-Colthurst, during the Easter Rising in April 1916, and Hanna campaigned for an inquiry into his death.
Historians now judge her a pioneer of Irish feminism whose life linked suffrage, nationalism and pacifism, and some note her criticism of the Irish Party’s position on women.

notes.h: Intermediate education and the payment-by-results system
notes.b: The Intermediate Education Act of 1878 set up a state-funded secondary system based on examinations and payment by results.
points: The Intermediate Education (Ireland) Act of 1878 created a state-funded system of secondary education, with a board that examined pupils and paid schools according to results.
Payment by results rewarded schools for pupils who passed examinations, which encouraged schools to prepare candidates for the exams.
The Intermediate system supported schools of different denominations, including Catholic convent schools and Protestant schools, and this helped to expand girls’ secondary education.
Girls’ schools, such as Alexandra College in Dublin, founded in 1866, used the Intermediate examinations to prepare pupils for higher education.

notes.h: The Royal University and women graduates (1879–1880)
notes.b: The Royal University of Ireland was set up in 1879 to award degrees to students from all denominations, and it admitted women to its degrees from 1880.
points: The Royal University of Ireland was established in 1879 as an examining body that awarded degrees to students from colleges of all denominations.
Women were admitted to the Royal University’s degrees from 1880, which gave women graduate status for the first time in Ireland.
The Royal University was criticised by Catholic bishops, who wanted a Catholic university, and this criticism led to the reforms of 1908.

notes.h: The Irish Universities Act and the language question (1900–1913)
notes.b: The 1908 Act created the National University of Ireland and Queen’s University Belfast, and the Gaelic League’s campaign for Irish in the schools and universities advanced in these years.
points: The Irish Universities Act of 1908 created the National University of Ireland, with constituent colleges in Dublin, Cork and Galway, and Queen’s University Belfast.
The Act responded to Catholic demands for a university with Catholic influence, while leaving Queen’s, the Protestant-dominated university, in Belfast.
The Revised Programme of Primary Instruction of 1900 allowed Irish to be taught in primary schools as a subject, which the Gaelic League had campaigned for.

notes.h: Assessment: the suffrage and education record
notes.b: Judgements on the period compare the progress of women’s public roles with the limits of the vote and the divisions within the movement.
points: Achievement: by 1898 women could sit on local boards, and the Royal University and the 1908 Act opened degrees to women and Catholic students.
Limit: Irish women did not win the parliamentary vote before 1918, and the Home Rule Bills of 1886, 1893 and 1912 did not include women’s suffrage.
Contemporary Irish Party leaders saw suffrage as a distraction from Home Rule, while suffragists saw the vote as a democratic right that should come first.
The movement was divided by nationalism and unionism, and its members differed over militancy; historians see this division as a source of both its energy and its weakness.
